CITIZEN PARTICIPATION PEPORT .
In September, 1966 Richmond's City Council adopted the Community Renewal Program (CRP) which presented a comprehensive study of the City and proposed action priorities. The area designated "Randolph Maymont" in the CRP received a high priority to carry out rehabilitation activities. Upon a request by City Council the Redevelopment and Housing Authority and its consultants prepared an application for a Survey and Planning grant from the Department of Housing and Urban Development, and in February, 1967, City Council approved the Survey and Planning application for the Randolph Conservation Project. When the application was sent to HUD, City Council realized that it may be some time before approval was received and planning could begin. Council, therefore, appropriated funds to make it possible for the Redevelopment and Housing Authority to begin detailed surveys of the area. In 1968, sanitarians from the City's Bureau of Environmental Health began a survey of the existing conditions of each property in the Randolph area, and collected necessary family and income information from the residents. Before the survey began, however, Redevelopment and Housing Authority representatives met with a group of Randolph area residents to discuss the survey with them and to determine whether or not a public meeting should be held to explain the purpose of the survey. This group, whose names were provided to the Redevelopment and Housing Authority by civic leaders knowledgeable with the Randolph area, decided that "'.. a public meeting should not be held at that time because of community feelings related to the announcement that a downtown expressway was being planned which would be built through the Randolph area. Residents of the area were violently opposed to the planned expressway and were relating the surveys by the Redevelopment and Housing Authority with the proposed expressway to be planned and constructed by the Richmond Metropolitan Authority.
On February 23, 1969, a public meeting was held at the Sixth Baptist Church in Randolph to present the results of the structural survey which had been completed. There was strong community opposition voiced toward the program. At this time Randolph's survey and planning application had still not been funded by HUD, and the Redevelopment and Housing Authority was converting programs in the Washington Park and Fulton areas of the City to the annual funding of the newly developed Neighborhood Development Program (NDP). HUD had indicated that the NDP was the only program being funded at that time. As a result of the meeting of February 23, 1969, the Redevelopment and Housing Authority notified the Randolph Community that it would not be included in the request for NDP funds. The Authority told the community that it would cooperate in any appropriate way in organizing the community so that they might formulate goals and objectives for the improvement of the neighborhood in accordance with plans to be developed by the citizens who live there.
At a second public meeting at the Second Baptist Church on April 8, 1969; the community voted to create a committee of twenty volunteers to discuss what action could be taken. The "Committee of Twenty" met on April 16, 1969, at the West End Richmond Community Action Program (RCAP) Center and officers were elected and boundary and publicity committees were formed.
The "Committee of Twenty" soon recognized that it did not have ample representation for the entire Randolph area. Therefore, the Boundary Committee set up districts around the schools in the area, and six districts were delineated, and residents from each district were asked to participate in developing a representative committee. On April 23, 1969, the name VOICES (Vehement Outcry of Interested Citizens for an Equitable Society) was adopted by an enlarged group, and officers were selected. The main task of the group was to organize and involve the Randolph citizens in a democratic election of a permanent organization to study the program and solicit community involvement.
